title: Level-by-level work in building a heap
summary: When building a heap, lower levels contain many more nodes, yet each node can sift down far fewer levels; summing the work by level yields a linear-time upper bound.
context: The figure analyzes heap construction using a perfect binary tree of height h: nodes are selected from bottom to top, and top-down heapification (sift-down) is applied to each node. Here “bottom up” refers to the order in which nodes are visited, while each repair still moves downward toward child nodes.

The tree is drawn on the left, while the two columns on the right are labeled “Node height (maximum number of sift-down iterations)” and “Number of nodes at each level,” aligned across levels by horizontal dashed lines. Leaf nodes have height 0 and the root has height h, where height counts edges down to the deepest leaf. The iteration count in the figure refers to the maximum number of levels a node can swap downward, excluding the final comparison check in code that confirms termination.
description: Let the root level have depth 0 and the leaf level have depth h. Level d has 2^d (2 to the power d) nodes, and each can sift down at most h − d levels; multiplying the two gives the upper bound for that level. Multiplying the total node count by the root height h would overestimate the total work, because roughly half the nodes are leaves that need no sifting down at all.

The figure lists the top four levels and the bottom two levels, separated by vertical ellipses; the table below adds the depth, general formula, and level-product columns. When h is small, only levels that actually exist apply, and top and bottom rows that coincide are not counted twice.
result: Summing across levels gives T(h) = 2^0×h + 2^1×(h−1) + … + 2^(h−1)×1 + 2^h×0. Shifting and subtracting in the accompanying text simplifies this to T(h) = 2^(h+1) − h − 2, where 2^(h+1) is 2 raised to the exponent (h plus 1). Since the total number of nodes is n = 2^(h+1) − 1, we obtain T(h) = n − h − 1; including linear overhead such as per-node checks, building a heap takes O(n) time.

In practice, sifting down can stop before reaching the upper bound whenever the heap property is satisfied early.
